newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha admits defeat in Albania elections.
newsitem.headline: Berisha admits defeat in Albania elections.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha conceded on Monday that his Democratic Party had lost Sunday's general election and international observers pronounced the polling "adequate and acceptable".
But Berisha kept Albanians guessing on whether the defeat meant he would resign as head of state.

His brief statement on state television, before official results had been declared, appeared to confirm that the Socialist Party swept to victory in the poll, called to restore order after months of unrest.

"Albanian voters yesterday seemingly voted that the Democratic Party should be in opposition. On this occasion I would like to express my deepest gratitude to those hundreds and thousands of Albanians...who supported the Democratic Party," Berisha said.
He urged members and sympathisers of his party "to treat yesterday's verdict with courage and dignity".

Catherine Lalumiere, the top official observing the election under the auspices of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said the vote had showed Albanians' desire for a democratic future despite minor flaws.

"We believe therefore that we can say that the elections can be considered as adequate and acceptable," she said. "The result of these elections can be the foundation for a stable, democractic system, which Albanians want and deserve."

The OSCE, together with the Council of Europe and a U.S. delegation, monitored Sunday's first round of the election. The head of the OSCE mission, former Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky was due in Albania on Tuesday.
Western European countries praised the vote.
Germany said Albanians had "expressed their will to return to orderly relations in an impressive way". France and Britain welcomed high turnout and relative calm.
Italian Prime Minister Roman Prodi had already on Sunday praised Italian soldiers, part of a 7,000-member international force dispatched in April, for helping keep the peace.

Albania's election commission announced complete returns in 11 of the country's 115 constituencies -- seven captured by Socialists and their allies and four going to run-off rounds next week after none of the candidates cleared 50 percent.
Election officials had already announced Socialist victories in some southern regions -- the heart of the armed rebellion which voted solidly against Berisha and his party.
Berisha's announcement was greeted with celebratory gunfire in the south but correspondents reported no serious incidents.
The interior ministry maintained a ban on demonstrations in Tirana pending publication of results. An armoured vehicle was stationed in Skanderbeg Square to show authorities meant business.

Berisha said he would respect all the commitments he made before and during the hard-fought campaign but it was unclear whether that meant he would step down. Many Albanians believe it is only a matter of time before he goes.
Democratic Party chairman Tritan Shehu said: "He has not resigned for the moment. But it all depends on him now."

Socialist Party leader Fatos Nano claimed a sweeping victory a few hours after polls closed on Sunday evening. The party says that once results of proportional voting are counted, Socialists and their allies will control almost two-thirds of seats in the 155-seat parliament.

A two-thirds majority would be enough to remove a head of state by parliamentary vote. Berisha, president since 1992 when the Democrats swept to power, has hinted on several occasions that he would quit if a leftist government came to power.

Released in March after three years in jail following a suspect trial, Nano said Albania should work towards altering political institutions. "Berisha lost his final chance for cohabitation with the Albanian people and the political forces that represent them," he said.
Interim Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, who took office in March when a 10-party coalition was formed to halt the choas, appealed to police and state officials to work responsibly.
More than 1,500 people have been killed in violence sparked by the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes in January.
